items.title: 30.4.3 Identifying O-H and N-H Protons by D2O Exchange

source_refs.note: Topic 30.4.3 with Quick Check 30.4, answered (PDF 209); an original before-and-after sketch is added. Answers need review.

blocks.text: Hydrogen atoms in O-H groups (alcohols, carboxylic acids) and N-H groups (amines, amides) are easily exchanged between molecules, so their singlet peaks show a wide range of chemical shifts and can be hard to identify. A technique called 'deuterium exchange', or the 'D2O shake', shows whether a singlet is due to an O-H or N-H hydrogen. First the 1H NMR spectrum of the compound is recorded, showing all its H atoms, including O-H or N-H. A few drops of D2O are then added to the sample tube, the solution is shaken well and the spectrum is recorded again. The O-H or N-H peak disappears in the second spectrum; comparing the two spectra identifies it.

The reason is that protons attached to highly electronegative atoms such as O or N are easily exchanged: when D2O is added, these hydrogens are quickly replaced by deuterium atoms, R-O-H + D2O <=> R-O-D + HOD. Deuterium needs a different energy for spin flipping, so it gives no peak in the 1H spectrum and becomes 'invisible'.

blocks.alt: Two sketches of the spectrum of ethanol. Before: an O-H singlet near 5.4 ppm, the CH2 quartet near 3.7 ppm and the CH3 triplet near 1.2 ppm. After shaking with a few drops of D2O: the CH2 and CH3 signals remain and the O-H signal is gone. Below: R-O-H + D2O <=> R-O-D + HOD.
blocks.caption: The D2O shake (original sketch for this topic).
blocks.long_description: Only the hydrogen on oxygen (or nitrogen) is exchanged for deuterium. Because deuterium does not absorb at the proton frequency, that one signal vanishes, while the signals of hydrogens on carbon are unchanged.

blocks.prompt: Why do O-H or N-H peaks disappear after a D2O shake?
blocks.explanation: The O-H or N-H hydrogens exchange with deuterium (R-O-H + D2O <=> R-O-D + HOD); deuterium absorbs at a different frequency, so it gives no 1H signal.

blocks.prompt: State the expected peak areas and splitting patterns for the -CH2CH2NH2 group.
blocks.explanation: Three signals with areas 2:2:2. The CH2 next to NH2 is a triplet (2 H on the neighbouring CH2); the NH2 is usually a broad singlet (and disappears with D2O); the other CH2 is at least a triplet, more if the rest of the molecule has H on its other neighbour.

items: O-H and N-H protons exchange with D2O and their signals vanish.
R-O-H + D2O <=> R-O-D + HOD; deuterium gives no 1H signal.
